background.definition: Narcolepsy is a neurological disorder characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness that waxes and wanes throughout the day with episodes of irresistible sleep. There are two major types of narcolepsy. Type 1 is narcolepsy with cataplexy. Type 2 is narcolepsy without cataplexy.

list.listitem: The prevalence is about 1.3 per 1000 persons in the United States.
The worldwide prevalence varies in different countries and is between 0.02 and 2 per 1000.
German patients with narcolepsy averaged $15,410 per patient per year in direct costs (medication, doctor visits, diagnostic tests, hospital charges, etc.).

These same patients averaged another $11,860 per patient per year in indirect costs, mostly from lost wages, and early retirement. Narcolepsy was listed as the cause of unemployment for almost half of the patients.
Medical services plus drug costs in the United States for patients with narcolepsy averaged $11,702 per patient per year, more than twice that of the general population
A single etiology for narcolepsy has not been established; however research suggests a combination of environmental factors and genetic factors.
First degree relatives have up to 75 times the risk of the general population of developing narcolepsy.
Monozygotic twins demonstrate limited concordance, implying that narcolepsy is a multifactorial condition.
A French case-control study reported an association between vaccination for H1N1 pandemic flu and the onset of narcolepsy/cataplexy.
Narcolepsy with cataplexy (Type 1 narcolepsy) is strongly associated with a deficiency of the neuropeptide hypocretin (or orexin) in the cerebrospinal fluid.
Over 70% of patients with type 1 narcolepsy have low hypocretin-1 in the CSF.
There is a strong link with certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) subtypes, specifically HLA DQB1 and HLA DR2.
There may be a subgroup of patients that are affected by an autoimmune mechanism, including a link to the pandemic influenza A H1N1 vaccine (Pandemrix) and to high anti-sterptococcal antibodies.
The diagnosis of narcolepsy can be made solely on a history of excessive daytime sleepiness and cataplexy. If there is no cataplexy, further sleep studies are required. C
Sleep studies to diagnose narcolepsy must include an overnight polysomnogram followed by a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT). C
A decreased CSF hypocretin level (≤110 pg/mL) is diagnostic for narcolepsy in the setting of increased daytime sleepiness and cataplexy. C

list.listitem: Excessive daytime sleepiness should be present on a nearly daily basis for at least three months. The Epworth sleepiness scale () is useful to measure daytime sleepiness and significantly correlates with sleep latency measured during the multiple sleep latency test (MSLT).

Cataplexy, a sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions, is characteristic of patients with narcolepsy. This may be mild, such as a jaw drop or head bob, or can be generalized with collapse to the ground. A history of cataplexy with excessive daytime sleepiness is nearly diagnostic.
Other historical features may include sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, nocturnal sleep disturbance, and automatic behaviors.
If narcolepsy is suspected, an overnight polysomnogram followed by a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) should be performed.
The MSLT starts 90 minutes to 3 hours after the overnight polysomnogram and consists of 5 naps at 2 hour intervals.

Two sleep onset REM periods (SOREMPS) during the MSLT support the diagnosis of narcolepsy. Sleep latency in patients with narcolepsy is decreased, usually less than 8 minutes, compared to control groups with a mean sleep latency of 10.5 minutes.

The MSLT has high specificity (97%) for narcolepsy, but is not very sensitive (70%). It is therefore helpful when abnormal for ruling in narcolepsy (LR+ 35), but less helpful to exclude it (LR− 0.31). It must therefore be interpreted along with historical and clinical findings.

HLA typing is not useful to confirm diagnosis, since the allele is also prevalent in up to 40% of the general population. The absence of the allele, however, may challenge the diagnosis of narcolepsy.
In patients with narcolepsy and cataplexy, hypocretin-1 levels in the CSF are less than 110 pg/ml, or one-third or the mean of a normal control. This may be used instead of a MSLT.
A detailed history, including a sleep diary, is key for diagnosing narcolepsy.
If narcolepsy is suspected, an overnight polysomnogram followed by a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) should be performed.
Initial treatment generally includes modafinil to improve alertness and sodium oxybate to reduce episodes of cataplexy.
Non-pharmacological treatments include planned daytime naps and appropriate selection of an occupation. C

European guidelines (2021) recommend pharmacotherapy for excessive daytime sleepiness. The most highly recommended drugs include modafanil, sodium oxybate, pitolisant and solriamfetol. Only sodium oxybate and antidepressants are recommended for treatment of cataplexy. For disordered nighttime sleep, only sodium oxybate is recommended. All of these drugs, and especially the stimulants, have potentially serious harms including cardiovascular effects for stimulants and respirator and CNS depression for sodium oxybate.
A network meta-analysis found the best balance of safety and benefit for pitolisant, sodium oxybate, and modafinil but the best overall efficacy for solriamfetol.
Modafinil (Provigil) 200 to 400 mg daily reduces daytime fatigue and is the drug of choice for narcolepsy. Modafinil does not control symptoms of cataplexy.

Modafinil may be given in divided doses. It promotes wakefulness, decreasing sleep attacks in up to 71% of narcoleptic patients. The most common modafinil side effects are headache (13%), nervousness (8%), and nausea (5%). About 9% of patients stop treatment because of adverse events.
Armodafinil (Nuvigil) is the longer-lasting isomer of modafinil. Dosed 50 to 400 mg daily.
Solriamfetol (Sunosi) may be a reasonable first-line option for daytime fatigue. It is dosed 75 to 150 mg in the morning.
Methylphenidate (Ritalin) 30 to 60 mg daily and other stimulants are second line agents.

Sodium oxybate (Xyrem) or low sodium oxybate in the form of mixed oxybate salts (Xywav) titrated to a goal of 6 to 9 g per night are the only USFDA medications approved for cataplexy and may be used in combination with modafinil. Both are administered in 2 doses separated by 2 to 4 hours. Start with 4.5 g per night and increase the dose every 1 to 2 weeks to goal of 6 to 9 g per night. The optimal response is usually seen in 8 to 12 weeks.Distribution is restricted due to serious potential adverse effects including respiratory depression, seizure, coma and death if abused. Information regarding permission to prescribe is found here from the manufacturer: www.xywavxyremrems.com

Extended-release sodium oxybate (Lumryz) was approved by the FDA in May 2023. It carries the same black box warning and has the same potential adverse effects as the shorter acting versions. Start with 4.5 g PO per night and increase by 1.5 g every week. Max dose 9 g/day. Distribution is restricted. See www.lumryzrems.com.

Fluoxetine (Prozac) 20 to 40 mg daily and a TCA, clomipramine 25 to 75 mg daily, have traditionally been recommended to treat cataplexy, however there is no evidence that antidepressants are of benefit in narcolepsy.
Long acting venlafaxine (37.5 to 150 mg daily) may help promote wakefulness and decrease cataplexy, however, not first line treatment.

Pitolisant, a histamine H3 receptor inverse agonist, has been licensed in the EU since 2016 and has recently been approved in the US. It holds promise in the treatment of cataplexy in patients with narcolepsy. It can prolong QT intervals though, especially in patients with hepatic or renal impairment.
Scheduled short naps are recommended by European guidelines (2021) with low quality evidence that they decrease sleepiness. However, this is insufficient as primary therapy for narcolepsy.

Other guideline recommended non-drug therapies include healthy lifestyle, exercise (which may increase hypocretin levels) and weight control. These are not supported by research, only expert opinion though.
In an uncontrolled study, a low carbohydrate ketogenic diet modestly improved daytime sleepiness.
Patients should be referred to a sleep lab for evaluation if narcolepsy is suspected by history.
Most patients require life long medications to control the excessive daytime sleepiness. C
Cataplexy may resolve spontaneously or with treatment.
Cataplexy may resolve spontaneously or with treatment.
Sleepiness may interfere with memory, concentration, and other cognitive abilities.
May have a profound impact on education, occupational choices, and social functioning.
Annually, 3% to 7% of patients with excessive daytime sleepiness will have a motor vehicle accident. B
Most patients require life long medications to control the excessive daytime sleepiness.
Excessive sleepiness is lifelong, although may decrease with age.
Cataplexy may resolve spontaneously or with treatment.
Hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis are usually temporary.
Disturbed nocturnal sleep usually does not improve.
Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT) tests the ability to stay awake. Not routinely used unless an objective measure of therapeutic response is needed, i.e., for driver's license in some states.
Regular follow up is advised to follow treatment efficacy.
Avoid smoking. The nicotine may worsen cataplexy.
Avoid driving while drowsy. Patient should not work as commercial drivers.
Older patients with narcolepsy are generally less sleepy.
It is important in the elderly to carefully look at other medications they may be taking that may mimic narcolepsy.
Careful choices in medication in general are important. Medications such as alpha blockers may exacerbate cataplexy.
Narcolepsy may worsen secondary to coexisting conditions such as sleep apnea.

Treatment of patients with narcolepsy during pregnancy is difficult. The safety of the medications used to treat narcolepsy is unknown, although Increased risk of teratogenic effects from medications for narcolepsy has not been demonstrated. All are pregnancy category C (animal studies have shown teratogenic or embryocidal effects, but there are no controlled studies in humans).
Risks of treatment vs. the benefits must be weighed. Ideally the medications would be stopped in pregnancy or at least the dose reduced.
With discontinuation of medications, some women are unable to work or drive for the duration of their pregnancy.
Narcolepsy is usually diagnosed in the teens and twenties, however, there have been rare cases described in infants and older adults.
Methylphenidate or modafinil are thought to be safe in children between 6 and 15 years of age.

Sitting and reading
Watching TV
Sitting, inactive, in a public place (e.g. a theater or a meeting or classroom)
As a passenger in a car for an hour without a break
Lying down to rest in the afternoon when circumstances permit
Sitting and talking to someone
Sitting quietly after a lunch without alcohol
In a car, while stopped for a few minutes in traffic
Total score:
Score
Interpretation
0-9 Normal
10-12 Borderline
13-24 Abnormal
How likely are you to doze off or fall asleep in the situations described below, in contrast to feeling just tired? This refers to your usual way of life in recent times. Even if you haven't done some of these things recently try to work out how they would have affected you. Use the following scale to choose the most appropriate number for each of the eight situations: 0 = would not doze, 1 = slight chance of dozing, 2 = moderate chance of dozing, and 3 = high chance of dozing.
